gloss: hundred; two hundred (dual); hundreds, a company of a hundred; a hundredfold
summary: מֵאָה is the number a hundred, a feminine noun with the construct מְאַת, the dual מָאתַיִם “two hundred” and the plural מֵאוֹת, which with the digits makes three hundred to nine hundred. Most of its uses are in counts: the years of the fathers from Adam (Gen 5; 11), the musters of the tribes (Num 1; 26), the returning families (Ezr 2; Neh 7), and the cubits, shekels and talents of the ark, the dwelling and the house (Gen 6:15; Exo 27:18; 38:27). The plural is also a body of men, the “hundreds” an army marches by and a captain is set over (Exo 18:21; 2Sa 18:4), and a hundred is scripture’s figure for many times over: Isaac’s “hundred measures”, a hundred blows, “a hundred times” (Gen 26:12; Pro 17:10; 2Sa 24:3). The Aramaic of Ezra and Daniel has the same word, מְאָה, and the Peshitta מָאא; Arabic miʾa, Ugaritic mit, Phoenician mʾt, Sabaic mʾt, Moabite mʾtn and Akkadian meʾatu are all “hundred”, and no verb or other sense of the root is known.

words.gloss: hundred; (dual) two hundred; (plural) hundreds, a company of a hundred
words.summary: The numeral a hundred: a feminine noun, absolute מֵאָה and construct מְאַת, standing before or after the thing counted (מֵאָה שָׁנָה, מְאַת שָׁנָה, אַמָּה מֵאָה). Its dual is מָאתַיִם, two hundred, and its plural מֵאוֹת, with the digits for three hundred and upward and by itself for the “hundreds” of an army. The written text of 2Ki 11:4, 9, 10 spells the plural המאיות, read הַמֵּאוֹת. The use count includes three tokens of הַמֵּאָה that are also filed as the name of a tower (Neh 3:1; 12:39; and Ezk 42:2, which is the plain number).

senses.definition: The number a hundred, counting years, people, animals, cubits and weights; alone, or joined to tens and units by וְ (“thirty and a hundred years”, “a hundred and twenty years”).

evidence.note: “A hundred talents of silver for casting the sockets … a hundred sockets for the hundred talents, a talent to a socket”: the count is checked against itself.
Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them “fifty men to a cave”: twice fifty. Again in 1Ki 18:13.
“Ten men of a hundred, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand”: the hundred in its place between ten and a thousand.
The court of the dwelling: its length מֵאָה בָאַמָּה, a hundred by the cubit, and its breadth fifty. So Exo 27:9, 11; 38:9, 11.
Jacob bought the portion of the field at Shechem for a hundred qesitah; Jos 24:32.
The fine for a bad name brought on a virgin of Israel: a hundred of silver.
Gideon and the hundred men with him, one of three companies of the three hundred.
Saul’s bride-price: a hundred foreskins of Philistines. David brought two hundred (18:27).
“How shall I set this before a hundred men?” They ate and left over.
The house of the forest of Lebanon: a hundred cubits its length.
A hundred cubits from gate to court in the house Ezekiel is shown; so 40:23, 27, 47; 41:13–15; 42:2, 8.
Ahasuerus reigned over “seven and twenty and a hundred” provinces; Est 8:9; 9:30.

senses.gloss: a hundred years: of a life or a span of time
senses.definition: A hundred in the count of a man’s years, most often as בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה “a son of a hundred years”, and of a length of time.

evidence.note: Abraham laughed: “Shall a child be born to a son of a hundred years (לְבֶן מֵאָה שָׁנָה)? And shall Sarah, a daughter of ninety years, bear?”
“Abraham was a son of a hundred years (בֶּן מְאַת שָׁנָה) when Isaac his son was born to him.”
Paul on Gen 17:17: Abraham did not weigh his own body, already dead, “being about a hundred years old”; the Peshitta has בַּר מָאא שְׁנִין, “a son of a hundred years”, the Hebrew idiom.
“Adam lived thirty and a hundred years (שְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה) and fathered a son in his likeness.”
Shem was a son of a hundred years when he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood.
“His days shall be a hundred and twenty years.”
Jacob to Pharaoh: “the days of the years of my sojournings are thirty and a hundred years; few and evil”.
Moses was a son of a hundred and twenty years when he died; Deu 31:2.
Joseph died a son of a hundred and ten years; so Joshua, Jos 24:29; Jdg 2:8.
Job lived after this a hundred and forty years.
Jehoiada died a son of a hundred and thirty years.
“The youth shall die a son of a hundred years, and the sinner, a son of a hundred years, shall be accursed.”
The waters prevailed on the earth fifty and a hundred days; Gen 8:3.

senses.definition: The dual, two hundred, used as the plural is with the higher digits.

evidence.note: Abigail took מָאתַיִם לֶחֶם, two hundred loaves, a hundred bunches of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs: dual and singular side by side.
Saul asked a hundred foreskins (18:25); David struck two hundred men of the Philistines.
David pursued with four hundred men; two hundred stayed behind, too faint to cross the brook Besor. The six hundred of 30:9 are the two together.
Jacob’s gift to Esau: two hundred she-goats, two hundred ewes.
The days of Terah were five years and two hundred years.
“The thousand is yours, Solomon, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.”
Two hundred singing men and women with the return; Neh 7:67 has two hundred and forty-five.
A thousand, two hundred and ninety days.

senses.gloss: hundreds (plural מֵאוֹת, with the digits: three hundred to nine hundred)
senses.definition: The plural after a digit in the construct (שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת “three hundreds”), for three hundred to nine hundred, and so in the great totals between the thousands and the tens.

evidence.note: The ark: three hundred cubits (שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת אַמָּה) its length, fifty its breadth, thirty its height.
Gideon divided the three hundred men into three companies; one of them is “the hundred men” with him (7:19).
All the numbered of Israel: six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty. The hundreds stand twice: over the thousands and in their own place.
All the days of Adam: nine hundred years and thirty years. Methuselah’s nine hundred and sixty-nine are the longest (5:27).
Abram’s seed afflicted four hundred years in a land not theirs.
The sojourning of the sons of Israel: thirty years and four hundred years.
About six hundred thousand on foot went out from Rameses.
The field of Machpelah: four hundred shekels of silver.
Seven hundred chosen men of Benjamin, left-handed, slinging at a hair.
The house begun in the four hundred and eightieth year after the going out from Egypt.
Solomon’s seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
The years of Israel’s iniquity given to the prophet as days: three hundred and ninety.
For the holy place five hundred by five hundred, square.
The whole assembly of the return: forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty.
“Until evening, morning, two thousand and three hundred.”

senses.gloss: a “hundred”: a company of men under its captain
senses.definition: A body of a hundred men, the division below the thousand by which Israel was judged and its armies were ordered, each under a שַׂר, a captain; the plural מֵאוֹת names the companies themselves, which march “by hundreds and by thousands”.

evidence.note: Jethro’s counsel: able men set over the people as “captains of thousands, captains of hundreds, captains of fifties and captains of tens”. Done in Exo 18:25; recalled in Deu 1:15.
“All the people went out by hundreds and by thousands (לְמֵאוֹת וְלַאֲלָפִים)”, after David had set captains of thousands and captains of hundreds over them (18:1).
The lords of the Philistines passed on “by hundreds and by thousands”.
Moses was angry with the officers of the army, “the captains of the thousands and the captains of the hundreds”; so 31:48, 52, 54.
Saul: “Will the son of Jesse make you all captains of thousands and captains of hundreds?”
Jehoiada took “the captains of the hundreds” of the Carites and the runners and showed them the king’s son; they carry out the plan (11:9, 10, 15, 19; 2Ch 23:1, 9, 14, 20).
David consulted the captains of the thousands and the hundreds; so 1Ch 28:1; 2Ch 1:2.
Amaziah set Judah in order by fathers’ houses, under captains of the thousands and captains of the hundreds.

senses.gloss: a hundred: many times over; a great or a full number
senses.definition: A hundred as the figure for a great increase or a great many: a hundred for one, a hundred times, a hundred set against five or ten or against a thousand.

evidence.note: “Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundred measures (מֵאָה שְׁעָרִים), and Yahweh blessed him”: a hundred for the one sown.
Joab: “May Yahweh your God add to the people, as they are and as they are, a hundred times (מֵאָה פְעָמִים).” So 1Ch 21:3.
The seed on good ground gave fruit, “some a hundred, some sixty, some thirty”: Isaac’s measure, as the top of the scale; explained in 13:23.
“A rebuke goes deeper into one who understands than striking a fool a hundred times.”
A sinner does evil a hundred times (מְאַת, with no noun) and prolongs his days.
“If a man father a hundred, and live many years … and his soul is not filled with good”.
“Five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred of you shall chase ten thousand.”
In judgment the reverse: the city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out a hundred shall have ten.
He who has left house or brothers for Jesus’ sake receives “a hundredfold now in this time”.

senses.gloss: “the hundred of” the silver: the hundredth part (?)
senses.definition: Once, of what the nobles were taking from their brothers on loans: מְאַת הַכֶּסֶף, “the hundred of the silver”, with the grain, the new wine and the oil. The construct with the article reads most simply as a rate, the hundredth, taken as interest; the text does not say for what period, and nothing else in scripture uses the word so.

evidence.note: “Give back to them today their fields, their vineyards, their olive yards and their houses, and the hundred of the silver and the grain, the new wine and the oil that you are exacting of them.” The charge is usury (5:7, 10).

senses.gloss: the Hundred: a tower on the wall of Jerusalem
senses.definition: With the article, the name of a tower on the north wall of Jerusalem, מִגְדַּל הַמֵּאָה “the tower of the hundred”, between the sheep gate and the tower of Hananel. The text does not say what hundred it was named for (cubits, or a company of a hundred).

evidence.note: Eliashib and the priests built the sheep gate and consecrated it “as far as the tower of the hundred, as far as the tower of Hananel”.
The second thanksgiving company passed the fish gate, “the tower of Hananel and the tower of the hundred, as far as the sheep gate”.

evidence.note: A man with a hundred sheep, one of them gone astray; Luk 15:4.
The seed that bore a hundred.

“A hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters … with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.”
The seed on good ground “bore fruit a hundredfold”: Gen 26:12’s hundred measures.

Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian cohort.

evidence.note: “Two hundred denarii of bread is not enough for them.”

parallels.note: “Thousand”, the next step up: captains of thousands and of hundreds, by hundreds and by thousands, a hundred of a thousand.
“Fifty”, the half and the next division down: captains of hundreds and of fifties; a hundred hidden by fifties; a hundred cubits by fifty.
“Ten”, the tenth of it: ten of a hundred; a hundred left of a thousand and ten of a hundred.
“Ten thousand”, as a hundred is to five: five chase a hundred, a hundred ten thousand.

opposites.note: “Five”, the few who put a hundred to flight.

a son of a hundred years: a hundred years old
a hundred by the cubit: a hundred cubits

words.summary: The Aramaic of Ezra and Daniel has the Hebrew’s word with its own vowels: מְאָה a hundred, dual מָאתַיִן two hundred, and for four hundred the digit with the singular, אַרְבַּע מְאָה, where Hebrew has the plural אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת.

senses.definition: The number a hundred, of animals offered, of talents and measures, and with twenty of Darius’ satraps.

evidence.note: At the dedication of the house of God: “a hundred bulls, two hundred rams (דִּכְרִין מָאתַיִן), four hundred lambs (אִמְּרִין אַרְבַּע מְאָה)”: one, two and four hundred in one verse.
Artaxerxes’ grant: up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred cors of wheat, a hundred baths of wine and a hundred baths of oil.
Darius set over the kingdom a hundred and twenty (מְאָה וְעֶשְׂרִין) satraps.

senses.definition: The dual מָאתַיִן, as Hebrew מָאתַיִם.

words.gloss: hundred; (dual מַאתֵין) two hundred; (in compounds) three hundred to six hundred
words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܡܐܐ (mā), a hundred, with ܡܐܬܝܢ (mātēn) two hundred. “A hundredfold” is חַד בַּמָאא, “one in a hundred”, and “by hundreds” is the word doubled, מָאא מָאא. SEDRA files the higher hundreds as lexemes under their digits: תְּלָתמָאא three hundred, אַרְבַּעמָאא four hundred, חַמֵשׁמָאא five hundred, שֵׁתמָאא six hundred.

evidence.note: “If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them strays, does he not leave the ninety-nine?”: a hundred is ninety-nine and one. Luk 15:4.
The debtor of a hundred baths of oil writes fifty; the debtor of a hundred cors of wheat, eighty (16:7).
A fellow servant owed him a hundred denarii.
About a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes.
The net full of great fish, a hundred and fifty-three.
About a hundred and twenty names together.
Abraham, “a son of a hundred years” (בַּר מָאא שְׁנִין), did not weaken in faith: Gen 17:17.
The sealed: a hundred and forty-four thousand of all the tribes of Israel; Rev 14:1, 3.
The city’s wall, a hundred and forty-four cubits.
“Two hundred denarii of bread is not enough for them, for each to take a little”; Mrk 6:37.
About two hundred cubits from the land.
Two hundred soldiers and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea.
Two hundred and seventy-six souls in the ship.
A thousand two hundred and sixty days; Rev 12:6.

senses.definition: The digit joined to מָאא in one word for the higher hundreds.

evidence.note: Stephen quotes Gen 15:13: his seed enslaved and ill-treated four hundred (אַרְבַּעמָאא) years.
The ointment might have been sold for more than three hundred denarii.
Two debtors: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty.
He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once.
About four hundred men joined Theudas.
The number six hundred and sixty-six.

senses.definition: The word doubled for companies of a hundred each, as the Hebrew’s “by hundreds”.

evidence.note: The five thousand sat down in ranks, “by hundreds and by fifties”.

senses.definition: “One in a hundred”: a hundred for one, of a harvest and of what is repaid to one who leaves all.

evidence.note: Everyone who has left houses or brothers or lands for my name “shall receive a hundredfold (חַד בַּמָאא) and inherit eternal life”.
Seed on good ground “made fruit one in a hundred (חַד בַּמָאא)”: a hundred grains for the one sown.
“A hundredfold now in this time … and in the age to come eternal life.”
The same harvest said with דְּ: “there was that of a hundred (דְּמָאא), and of sixty, and of thirty”; explained of the one who hears the word and understands it (13:23). Mrk 4:8, 20.

cognates.note: The same three forms as the Hebrew: singular for a hundred, dual for two hundred, plural with a digit for three hundred and above. Ugaritic keeps the feminine t in the singular, which Hebrew and Aramaic have dropped outside the construct (מְאַת).

evidence.note: “The numeral ‘100’ occurs in the singular for ‘100,’ and in the dual for ‘200’; in the plural it is used with the appropriate digit for ‘300’ and above”; the dual mitm compared with Arabic miʾatāni and Hebrew māʾtayim. Examples: mit.pḥm, mit.iqni “100 gems, 100 (pieces of) lapis lazuli” (KTU 3.1:27–28); ḫmšm.l.mitm.zt “250 olive trees” (KTU 4.143:2). Read from the OCR text; check the page image.

doctrine.statement: Genesis gives the fathers from Adam to Noah one by one, each with the years he had lived when his son was born, the years he lived after, and the sum: “Adam lived thirty and a hundred years and fathered a son … and all the days of Adam that he lived were nine hundred years and thirty years, and he died” (Gen 5:3–5). The line runs unbroken to Noah, who “was a son of six hundred years when the flood of waters was on the earth” (Gen 7:6), and the flood itself is dated to the month and day of that year (Gen 7:11). After the flood the same count runs on from Shem, “a son of a hundred years” two years after it, to Terah and Abram (Gen 11:10–26). The New Testament reads the list as a real descent: Luke carries Jesus’ line back through these same names to “Adam, of God” (Luk 3:36–38), and Jude calls Enoch “the seventh from Adam” (Jud 1:14), which is his place in Gen 5. Jesus puts the making of man and woman at “the beginning of the creation” (Mrk 10:6). From the verses: scripture counts the years from the first man by fathers and sons, with no gap left to fill, so that man’s time on the earth, and the earth’s own since the six days, is numbered in thousands of years and not in ages.

When God promised Abraham a son by Sarah, Abraham “fell on his face and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born to a son of a hundred years? And shall Sarah, a daughter of ninety years, bear?” (Gen 17:17). The child was born as promised: “Abraham was a son of a hundred years when Isaac his son was born to him” (Gen 21:5). Paul takes the hundred years as the measure of what Abraham believed against: he “did not consider his own body, already dead, being about a hundred years old, nor the deadness of Sarah’s womb … but was strong in faith, giving glory to God, and fully persuaded that what he had promised he was able also to do; therefore it was counted to him for righteousness” (Rom 4:19–22). Hebrews says the same: “from one, and him as good as dead”, came a multitude like the stars (Heb 11:11–12). Paul adds that it was written for us also, “who believe on him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead” (Rom 4:23–24). From the verses: the faith counted for righteousness is belief that God gives life where there is none, first in a body a hundred years old, and then in raising the dead.

Isaiah’s “new heavens and new earth” are described on the ground: Jerusalem made a rejoicing, houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and eaten (Isa 65:17–19, 21–22). In it “there shall no more be an infant of days, nor an old man who does not fill his days; for the youth shall die a son of a hundred years, and the sinner, a son of a hundred years, shall be accursed” (Isa 65:20), and “as the days of a tree are the days of my people” (65:22). So in that time men still sin and still die, but a death at a hundred is the death of a youth. The same chapter has the wolf and the lamb feeding together “in all my holy mountain” (65:25), the words Isaiah uses of the reign of the shoot from Jesse’s stem, who judges the poor of the earth (Isa 11:1–9). Paul sets the order: Christ “must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet; the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death” (1Co 15:25–26). From the verses: the kingdom is on the earth, at Jerusalem, over mortal nations whose lives are lengthened, and death, still present under Christ’s reign, is done away only at its end.

Isaac sowed in a land of famine where he had been told to stay, “and found in that year a hundred measures, and Yahweh blessed him” (Gen 26:1–3, 12). Jesus uses the same figure twice. Of the word sown: the seed on good ground is “he who hears the word and understands it, who bears fruit and yields, one a hundred, one sixty, one thirty” (Mat 13:8, 23). And of what is given up for him: no one has left house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, wife, children or lands “for my sake and the gospel’s, but he shall receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mrk 10:29–30). From the verses: the hundredfold is the present return, the household of those who believe, given along with persecutions; eternal life is named apart from it and is placed in the age to come.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. Root key מאה as the database keys it (BDB m.ac); no other entry has it. A noun with no verbal root: no verb or other sense is attested in Hebrew or the cognates (Arabic مأى “mew”, “stretch” in Lane p. 3016 is unrelated and not recorded). BDB keys: m.ac.aa (the numeral, 581 tokens) and xm.aa.ab (Aramaic, 8 tokens: Dan 6:2; Ezr 6:17 three times; Ezr 7:22 four times). m.ac.ab is הַמֵּאָה, the tower of Neh 3:1; 12:39: a place, so no name entry; its three tokens are the same occurrences as m.ac.aa (and its third, Ezk 42:2, is the plain number), so the key is not named and the tower is a sense of the numeral. m.ad.ag מְאָיוֹת is a cross-reference with no tokens: the ketiv המאיות of 2Ki 11:4, 9, 10 (the database’s ketiv table; 11:15 not listed there). No name entries: the root forms no personal name. Peshitta: SEDRA root מאא, lexemes 1697 מאא and 1698 מאתינ, found through the database’s nt_word table; the compounds 3400 תלתמאא, 269 ארבעמאא, 1078 חמשמאא, 3334 שתמאא are filed by SEDRA under their digits and folded into מָאא here, as chamesh and shesh mention them from their side. Syriac pointing follows SEDRA’s vocalised forms (מָאא, מַאתֵין). Greek: MACULA’s file spells ἑκατοντάρχους with ξ for χ and gives no lemma, so the lemma ἑκατόνταρχος is the New Testament’s; ἑκατονταέτης (Rom 4:19) is not recorded because MACULA leaves Gen 17:17’s מֵאָה unaligned, as it does Gen 26:12’s. Neh 5:11 מְאַת הַכֶּסֶף: taken as the hundredth (a rate of interest) with a question mark; some read מַשַּׁאת “the debt of”, not followed. Not written: any doctrine from Gen 6:3 (whether the hundred and twenty years are the time left before the flood or a limit of life the text does not settle in so many words), from the four hundred and four hundred and thirty years (Gen 15:13; Exo 12:40; Gal 3:17), which belong with the sojourning, or from Daniel’s 2,300, 1,290 and 1,335 days and the Revelation’s 144,000 and 1,260 days, which belong to prophecy. Leads not followed: Ge’ez məʾət and Tigre, Tigrinya forms (Fisher 1969 p. 122 or 123 has the comparison but the OCR is unreadable; Dillmann and Leslau not consulted); Mesha line 29 (מאת “hundred” of towns) not checked against Compston; CAL and Payne Smith for the Aramaic and Syriac. Segert pp. 53–54 and 191, Krahmalkov pp. 268 and 439 and Biella pp. 265–266 were read from the OCR text and page markers only; check the page images.
